newsitem.title: UK: Nigerian oil seen softer after low trade.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian oil seen softer after low trade.

text.p: West African grades were seen a shade softer on Wednesday after a Nigerian cargo traded at a low price a day earlier, while better margins were giving short-term support to Russian Urals, traders said.

West Africa was quiet early in the day but traders said some pressure would set in after a Brass River (June 22-24) was reported sold by a U.S. oil company to a trading house at Dated Brent +33 cents late on Tuesday.

The price was about 20 cents lower than last done in the sweet Nigerian grade. The seller was reported to have been asking a 45 to 58 cents premium to Dated Brent up to Monday, before selling at a distressed price.
Bonny Light was assessed a few cents weaker in the Dated Brent plus mid forties region while Forcados was in the Dated Brent +20 cents area, also a few cents off.
Traders said there were some eight unsold June cargoes still left, including Qua Iboe, Bonny Light, Forcados and Odudu.
"This deal makes you think twice before paying the numbers the sellers are asking for," one trader said, adding that most buyers were on the sidelines at the moment, waiting for the dust to settle.

"I expect the differentials to come off a bit before we see the July barrels being traded...because of the June avails and North Sea (grades)are coming off a bit which is putting a little bit of pressure on West African," the trader said.

Some traders also saw competition coming in from North African grades, namely Saharan Blend, which was being offered by Algeria's state oil company Sonatrach to European traders at Dated Brent plus low fifties.
But other traders were more positive, saying that Brass was a very buyer-specific grade and thus its trading levels should not always be taken as an indicator for the whole market.

"Brass is one of those grades with limited potential homes, and not that many cargoes come out every month," a trader said, adding the Brass cargo would not have found a buyer in the U.S. Gulf, the traditional home for West African barrels.
But he added: "Certainly the market has not strengthened, I would say it is steady to a shade softer."
In the Mediterranean, stronger refining margins were offering some short-term support to Russian Urals but the spectre of fresh Iraqi Kirkuk exports was likely to cap gains, traders said.
A cargo was traded on Tuesday at Dated Brent -$1.31 c+f Italy, around 10 cents firmer than deals done last week.
"With the fall in the flat (Brent) price and in Dated, margins are looking much better," a trader said.
Another large cargo was heard traded on Tuesday at Dated Brent -$1.32 and a small cargo at Dated Brent -$1.33, but these deals could not be confirmed.
But traders said that the early June period was now looking fairly tight, especially for large cargoes.
"If a west Med refiner wants to get hold of a large ship before the 13th or 14th there isn't much to chose from," said one.

But traders said that the poor performance of high sulphur fuel oil relative to low sulphur plus the expected renewal of the Iraqi oil-for-food agreement with the United Nations was tempering bullish sentiment in the sour market.
"I can't see anything that would pull the market much higher with Kirkuk looking like it's around the corner, but a lot depends on timing," a trader said.
-Haitham Haddadin, Ros Russell, +44 171 542 8145
